guides/how-to-take-a-photo-for-a-job-app.h1: How to Take a Photo for a Job Application at Home: a 2026 Expert Guide

sections.title: How to Take a Photo for a Job Application at Home: a 2026 Expert Guide
items: Want to know how to take a photo for a job application at home? Use a plain background, soft light from a window, and a phone placed at eye level about 4–6 feet (1.2–1.8 m) away. Take a head-and-shoulders photo, looking into the lens with a natural expression. Save it in the size and format requested by the employer or job platform. Use the PhotoGov Resume photo maker to adjust the image or create professional business looks with a casual-to-formal clothes change service. For a small square image, our 1x1 photo tool crops the file to that format.

sections.title: How to Take a Job Application Photo at Home: 8 Steps
items: You’re planning to apply for a new job and need to update your CV? This simple task suddenly comes with a long list of questions. What kind of photo to attach? What background should you use? Should you smile? What should you wear? Is a phone camera good enough?

The good news is that you don’t need a studio or a professional photographer. A plain wall, soft window light, and a smartphone are enough to take a professional photo at home. This guide walks you through the process, from choosing the right format to making, editing, and submitting the image.

sections.title: Step 1: Check the Photo Requirements
items: Before you take the photo, open the application or upload page and check what the employer or platform asks for. Photo requirements vary, and the instructions on that page always come first. Write down:
the required width and height;
the shape of the photo: square, vertical, or circular;
the accepted file type, such as JPG or PNG;
the maximum file size;
any rules for the background, clothing, or expression.

If no dimensions are listed, take a high-resolution head-and-shoulders photo with some extra space around you. You can crop it later for LinkedIn, an employer portal, a company profile, or a printed CV. When a form asks for a 30x40 photo size , the same portrait can be converted to it later.

sections.title: Step 2: Find a Plain Background
items: Find a smooth wall in white, light gray, beige, or another soft neutral color. Remove pictures, shelves, plants, door frames, and anything else that may appear behind you.

Stand at least 3 feet (1 m) away from the wall. This keeps your shadow off the background and gives the photo a cleaner, more professional look. If you don’t have a suitable wall, use a large piece of matte poster board or a smooth sheet with no visible folds.
Choose clothing that stands out from the background. A light shirt can disappear against a white wall, while a medium or dark color creates a clearer outline.

sections.title: Step 3: Use Soft, Even Light
items: Stand near a large window with the light coming from in front of you or slightly from the side. This gives your face soft, even light and keeps both eyes clearly visible.

Direct sunlight is usually too harsh. Move farther from the window or use a thin curtain if you see bright spots on the skin, deep shadows, or squinting. Turn off warm ceiling lights while using daylight so your skin tone stays consistent across the photo.
If you’re wearing glasses, take a test shot and check the lenses. Moving the light a little higher or farther to the side is often enough to remove glare.
For an evening photo, place two similar lamps near the camera, one on each side and slightly above eye level. Bounce the light off a pale wall if the shadows look too strong.

sections.title: Step 4: Set Up Your Phone
items: Clean the camera lens with a soft cloth. Place the phone on a tripod, shelf, or stable stack of books, and use the regular 1× camera. The ultra-wide lens can stretch facial features when the phone is close.

Keep the camera at eye level and about 4–6 feet (1.2–1.8 m) from your face. This distance gives you more natural facial proportions than an arm’s-length selfie. Use a timer, a remote shutter, or ask someone to take the photo for you.

The main rear camera often gives you the clearest image, especially indoors. A front camera can also work if the photo is sharp. Turn off beauty filters, skin smoothing, face reshaping, and any setting that changes your appearance.
Regular photo mode is the safest option. If you use Portrait mode, zoom in after the shot and check the edges of your hair, glasses, and shoulders for blur or cutout marks.

sections.title: Step 5: Get the Framing Right
items: Frame the photo from the upper chest or shoulders to just above the head. Keep your full head, neck, and both shoulders in the picture, with a small amount of space above your hair.
Place your face near the center and keep the phone level. Look directly into the lens. A slightly wider photo is easier to crop later, especially if the platform displays it as a circle.
Take one test photo and preview it in the shape you need. Check that the top of the head, chin, and shoulders remain visible after cropping.

sections.title: Step 6: Choose What to Wear
items: Wear the same type of outfit you would wear to a good first meeting in your field. A jacket may suit a law, finance, consulting, or senior role. A neat shirt, blouse, knit top, or simple overshirt may feel more natural for technology, education, health care, design, hospitality, or a startup.
Solid colors and subtle patterns photograph well. Choose a color that contrasts with the background, and check the collar, shoulders, lint, and wrinkles before the photo.
Keep jewelry simple and logos small. Your clothes should support the impression you want to make while keeping the attention on your face.

sections.title: Step 7: Find a Natural Pose and Expression
items: Sit or stand tall with your shoulders relaxed. Keep your head upright and bring your chin slightly forward and down. You can turn your shoulders a little if it feels natural, while keeping both eyes clearly visible.

A small, genuine smile works well for most professional profiles and company pages. A calm neutral expression may suit a more formal application. Choose the expression that feels natural for your field and still looks like you.
Take a slow breath before the timer starts. This helps your face and shoulders relax, which makes the photo look more confident and approachable.

sections.title: Step 8: Take Several Photos and Choose the Best One
items: Take 15–20 photos with small changes in your smile, chin position, and shoulder angle. Pause between groups, look away from the camera, blink, and reset your posture.
Review the photos at full size. Check that:
both eyes are sharp;
the glasses have no glare;
the skin tone looks natural;
the shoulders look even;
the background is clean;
the expression feels relaxed;
the photo looks like you today.
Choose the photo that feels clear, current, and professional. A natural image will serve you better than the most heavily posed or edited one.

sections.title: How to Edit and Save Your Job Application Photo
Keep the Editing Light
items: You can adjust the crop, brightness, white balance, and contrast. These changes help the photo look clean while keeping your appearance true to life.

Keep your natural skin texture, facial features, hairline, and body proportions. One-tap headshot filters and AI tools can change small details in ways that become obvious during an interview or video call.

sections.title: Save the Right File
items: Keep the original photo, then save a separate version for each platform. Use the file type, dimensions, and size limit listed on the upload page.

JPG is the most common choice for online applications. PNG is also accepted by some platforms. For digital uploads, the pixel dimensions matter more than the DPI number. DPI becomes important when the instructions specify a physical print size.
Open the saved file before uploading it. Check the sharpness, crop, file size, and filename one last time.

sections.title: Prepare the Photo With PhotoGov
items: PhotoGov can prepare the crop and file size once you have chosen your best photo. Select the resume photo format requested by the employer or platform, upload the original, and review the preview before downloading. For a square centimeter format, our 4x4 cm photo tool resizes the same portrait to that size.

Use the square 2×2-inch resume photo tool for a square file and the 35×45 mm resume photo tool when a vertical format is requested. Keep the downloaded file together with the original so you can create another size later. That square is also listed as a 2x2 photo in cm , for employers who ask in centimeters.
The vertical option is prepared by our 35x45 mm photo tool , which is also used for passports and Schengen visas.
Add a Premium Business Clothes Option for a Professional Look

PhotoGov’s recent Premium casual-to-formal clothes feature is especially handy in job applications. After you upload your correctly taken selfie, the online passport photo maker can automatically replace your outfit with stylish business looks. An initial add-on includes 5 professional looks, and you can get 9 more for a little extra.

sections.title: Quick Check Before You Upload
items: The file type and size match the upload instructions.
The photo has the correct shape and dimensions.
Your eyes and face are sharp.
The light is even across your face.
The background is plain and free of shadows.
Your glasses have no glare.
Your head and shoulders fit comfortably inside the crop.
The photo reflects your current appearance.
The saved file opens correctly.

sections.title: Should You Include a Photo in a US Job Application?
items: In the United States, most private-sector resumes do not include a photo. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission advises employers to request only information needed to assess whether a person is qualified for the job and says employers should not ask applicants for a photograph before an offer is made and accepted.

You may still need a professional photo for LinkedIn, MyERAS, a company profile, an employer portal, a portfolio, or a role where appearance is part of the application. Use the guidance below to place the photo correctly.

sections.title: Private-Sector Resume
items: Leave the photo off a standard US resume unless the employer clearly requests one. When an application includes a separate photo field, upload the image there and follow the listed requirements.

sections.title: Federal Resume and USAJOBS
items: USAJOBS tells applicants to leave photos of themselves out of federal resumes and profiles. Keep your professional headshot on LinkedIn or your portfolio rather than adding it to the federal application.

sections.title: LinkedIn Profile Photo
items: LinkedIn accepts JPG and PNG profile photos from 400 × 400 pixels up to 7,680 × 4,320 pixels, with a maximum file size of 8 MB. Keep your face near the center and leave some space around your head because LinkedIn displays the image as a circle in many places.

sections.title: MyERAS Photo
items: The AAMC accepts JPG/JPEG or PNG photos up to 150 KB and asks applicants to keep the face centered. Programs most often use the photo to identify applicants when they arrive for an interview, so choose a clear, current image with natural editing.

sections.title: Employer Portals, International CVs, and Casting Applications
items: Follow the instructions on the application page. An employer portal may request a square headshot, an international CV may use a vertical portrait, and a casting notice may ask for a specific headshot or full-body image.
Save one high-resolution original and create the required version for each application.

sections.title: Common Job Application Photo Mistakes
items: Camera Too Close . A camera held at your arm’s length can make the center of the face look larger. Place the phone on a tripod with the rear camera up front, move it 4–6 feet away, and use the timer.

Shadow on the Background . A shadow on the background can throw off the whole image, making your face poorly visible and the whole shot unprofessional. Stand at least 3 feet from the wall and keep the main light near the camera.
Mixed Lighting . Window light and warm room light can give each side of the face a different color. Use daylight on its own or use lamps with the same color temperature.

Tight Crop . A close crop leaves little room for a square, circle, or vertical version of your business shot. Keep a wider original that shows your head and shoulders with sufficient space around them.

Heavy Editing . Strong skin smoothing, face reshaping, artificial hair, and generated clothing can make the photo look less credible. Do not overuse the editing; keep the photo looking as natural as possible.
Old Photo . Use an image that matches your current hairstyle, facial hair, glasses, and overall appearance. Update it after a noticeable change.
One File for Every Platform . LinkedIn, MyERAS, employer portals, and printed CVs may use different dimensions and file-size limits. Save a separate version for each one.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
Should I Put a Photo on My Resume in the United States?
items: No. Most US private-sector resumes do not include a photo. Use your professional picture on LinkedIn, a portfolio, or in a corporate profile. Add one to an application when the employer provides a photo field or clearly asks for a separate image. USAJOBS requires applicants not to attach a photo on federal resumes.

sections.title: Can I Take a Job Application Photo With My Phone?
items: Yes. A smartphone can produce a professional photo when the lens is clean, the phone is stable, the light is soft, and the camera is placed at eye level. A simple home setup is enough for most online profiles and employer portals.

sections.title: Which Phone Camera Should I Use for My CV Photo?
items: The main rear camera provides the clearest and sharpest shot — but you have to place it on a tripod or ask someone to take a photo. A good front camera can also work — but only if there is sufficient lighting, the background is plain, and you hold it steady at arm's length. Turn off beauty filters, skin smoothing, and portrait mode. Take a few shots, choose the best one, and use it for your application.

sections.title: What Background Is Best for a Job Application Photo?
items: A plain white, light gray, beige, or soft neutral background works well for most professional photos. Use the background color listed by the employer when one is specified. Be mindful of your clothing: it’s not good if it blends with the backdrop, so choose an outfit in contrasting colors.

sections.title: How Far Should the Camera Be From My Face?
items: When using a rear camera, place the phone on a tripod about 4–6 feet (1.2–1.8 m) away. This results in more natural facial proportions than an arm’s-length selfie and leaves enough space for a head-and-shoulders crop.

sections.title: Should I Smile in a Professional Photo?
items: A natural smile works well for LinkedIn, company profiles, and most professional headshots. A calm neutral expression may suit a formal application. Choose the expression that feels appropriate for your field and comfortable for you.

sections.title: What Should I Wear for a Job Application Photo?
items: Wear the same type of outfit you would wear to a good first meeting in your field. Solid colors and subtle patterns are easy to photograph. Choose clothes that fit well, contrast with the background, and highlight your face.

sections.title: Can I Wear Glasses in My Job Application Photo?
items: Yes. If you wear glasses every day, they can stay on. Move the window or lamps until your eyes are clearly visible through the lenses and the reflections disappear.

sections.title: Can I Use a Selfie for My Job Application Photo?
items: Yes. A phone is perfectly suitable, but the photo will look more natural when the camera is placed on a stand several feet away. Use a timer or ask someone to take the photo so you have enough room for a clean crop.

sections.title: What Size Should a Job Application Photo Be?
items: There is no universal size for a job application photo. Follow the dimensions, shape, file type, and file-size requirements listed by the employer or platform. LinkedIn and MyERAS, for example, use different technical requirements.

sections.title: How Much Editing Is Acceptable for a Job Application or CV Photo?
items: Crop, brightness, white balance, and light contrast adjustments are usually enough. Do not use beauty filters or AI enhancers. Keep your facial features, skin texture, hairline, and body proportions true to life so the photo still looks like you.

sections.title: Can I Use an AI-Generated Headshot?
items: Better not. A recent real photo is the safest choice for an application. AI-generated headshots can slightly change facial features, hair, clothing, or proportions. Use a genuine photo with simple technical corrections for sizing, crop, and framing.

sections.title: How Recent Should the Job Application Photo Be?
items: Use a photo that reflects your current appearance. Take a new one after a noticeable change in hairstyle, facial hair, glasses, or another feature that affects how easily people recognize you.

sections.title: How Do I Make a Job Application Photo With PhotoGov?
items: Take a clear head-and-shoulders photo, choose the PhotoGov resume photo format requested by the employer or platform, upload the original, and review the crop. Download the digital or printable file, and submit it with your application.

guides/how-to-take-a-student-id-photo.h1: How to Take a Student ID Photo for US Colleges and Universities (2026)

sections.title: How to Take a Student ID Photo for US Colleges and Universities (2026)
items: Congratulations — you're officially a college student. Now comes one of the first real tasks on your pre-arrival checklist: submitting your student ID photo. This is the picture that goes on your campus card, the one you'll be flashing at the library, the gym, the dining hall, and pretty much everywhere else on campus for the next few years — so it's worth getting right. If your school specifically requests a square 2x2 image, our 2x2 photo maker provides a separate option.

The good news is you don't need a studio or a photographer. Most US universities let you upload your ID photo online before you even set foot on campus, and your smartphone is more than enough to do the job. This guide walks you through exactly how to take a student ID photo that clears first-time review, based on official card office requirements from Harvard, the University of Iowa, the University of Houston, and NC State.

sections.title: What Is a US Student ID Photo and Where Is It Used?
items: A US college or university student ID photo is a formal photograph submitted to your institution's card office as part of the process of obtaining your campus ID card (often called a Hawk Card, One Card, HawkCard, Wolfpack Card, CUID, or your school's equivalent). Unlike a social profile picture, a student ID photo is an official institutional identification document.
Your student ID photo is not only printed on your physical campus card — it is also typically stored in your institution's identity management system and may be visible to:
Course instructors and teaching staff, who use it to match names to faces in their rosters
Academic advisors and administrative staff
Campus security and police, for identity verification
Exam proctoring and academic integrity systems
Library, dining, and building access systems
University directories and degree audit portals

Because your photo appears in multiple official systems beyond the physical card, universities treat it as a formal identification photograph rather than a casual profile image. Submitting a poor-quality, filtered, or non-compliant photo can result in rejection and delay your card pickup — which in turn may delay access to buildings, dining plans, transit passes, and library services that are tied to the card.

There is no single national standard for US student ID photos. Every college and university sets its own specifications. Always check your institution's card office website before submitting. This guide covers the requirements that appear consistently across US institutions and gives you the safest defaults when your school's requirements are not fully specified.

sections.title: How to Take a Compliant Student ID Photo at Home: 6 Steps
items: Step 1: Set up your background

Find a smooth, solid white or light-colored wall. White is the safest choice — a white student ID photo background is accepted by all schools. Light gray or beige is accepted by some but not all institutions.

If your walls are not a suitable color, tape a clean, flat sheet of white foam board, poster board, or printer paper to a wall. The surface must be completely smooth — even light wrinkles or creases create shadow lines that appear in photos.

Stand at least 3 feet (1 meter) from the background. At this distance, your body does not cast a shadow onto the wall behind you. Shadows on the student ID photo are the most common cause of background shadow rejection.
Remove all objects, furniture, artwork, and items visible behind you. The background must show only a single solid color.
Step 2: Set up your lighting
Position yourself near a large window — it has to be on the side, or in front of you, but not behind. This produces soft, even lighting across both sides of your face.
If using artificial lighting: place two lamps at 45-degree angles on either side of your camera, at face level. This eliminates shadows under the eyes, nose, and chin.
Avoid overhead lighting — it creates shadows under the eyes and the chin. Don’t use flash.
Check for even lighting on both sides of your face before shooting. In a mirror or on-screen preview, both sides of your face should appear equally lit with no visible shadow.
Step 3: Set up your camera

Use your phone's rear camera — not the front-facing selfie camera. Rear cameras on modern smartphones capture at 36–48 megapixels with accurate color rendering. Front cameras capture at 12 megapixels and automatically apply beauty and skin-smoothing modes.

In your camera app settings, turn off: Portrait mode, HDR, Live Photo, Beauty mode, AI face enhancement, and any filter or skin-smoothing option. These features alter the photo in ways that university card offices explicitly prohibit.
Set the camera at eye level — not tilted up at you, as it makes the face look distorted, and not angled down at you, as it shrinks the face. Eye level produces a neutral, accurate image.
Use a tripod, a book stack, or prop your phone securely. Set a 3-second self-timer to avoid blur from pressing the shutter.
Step 4: Frame the shot correctly

Your framing must show: the top of your head (with a small gap above it — your head should not touch the edge of the frame), your full face, neck, and both shoulders. The bottom of the frame should be cut at approximately collarbone level.
Your face should be centered in the frame. Look at the preview: your nose should be at the vertical center of the image, and your face should be roughly centered horizontally.

Do not crop so tightly that only your face appears — the shoulders must be visible. Do not frame so wide that you appear very small in the image — your face should fill a significant portion of the frame.
Step 5: Position and expression
Face the camera directly. Both ears should be at the same height. No head tilt, no rotation to one side, no profile or three-quarter angle.
Both eyes must be fully open and clearly visible. Brush your hair away from your face before shooting — hair covering an eye is grounds for rejection at most institutions.

Expression: natural and composed. Most US schools permit a mild smile. An open-mouthed smile is not recommended. A forced or strained expression is not recommended. The most accepted expression is natural and relaxed.
Remove hats, beanies, bandanas, and sports team headwear. Religious head coverings are permitted; ensure your full face is clearly visible from forehead to chin.
Step 6: Shoot, review, and export
Take at least 10–15 shots. Micro-expressions, slight posture shifts, and eye positions change between frames in ways that are invisible in the moment but visible at full resolution.

Review each photo at full zoom on your phone. Check: both eyes fully open, even lighting on both sides of the face, no shadow on the background, face centered, no motion blur, hair away from the eyes.

Export the best photo as JPEG. If your school has a file size limit, compress the export: a JPEG at quality setting 75–80 (on a scale of 1–100) typically produces a file of 60–200 KB from a head-and-shoulders crop. Do not apply any editing, filters, or adjustments to the exported file. Crop to the correct framing before exporting, then stop. No retouching.
Use the PhotoGov student photo tool to create a compliant image that doesn’t require any adjustments and can be submitted right away.

sections.title: What to Wear for Your Student ID Photo
items: Your clothing choice affects the overall impression from your photo, as well as its official acceptance. One rule overrides all others: do not wear white or off-white clothing if your background is white.
Colors that work well
Navy, dark blue, charcoal, black, and deep jewel tones (teal, burgundy, forest green) all photograph cleanly against a white or light neutral background.
Medium blues, purples, and greens are strong options. They contrast well with most background colors and most skin tones.
Solid colors are always preferable to patterns. Stripes, plaids, and prints create visual noise that draws attention away from your face.
Clothing to avoid
White, cream, ivory, or any light-colored top that may blend with your background.

Tube tops, spaghetti straps, and backless tops — some schools explicitly reject photos where the student appears bare-shouldered, as it can look as if they are not wearing a top at all in the cropped ID format.
Clothing with large logos, slogans, sports insignia, or team branding.
Shiny or reflective fabrics that create hotspots under lighting.
General appearance
Wear what you would wear to class on a normal day — neat and presentable, not formal. A student ID photo does not require professional or business attire.
Jewelry: keep it simple. Small earrings and a necklace are fine; large statement pieces may create glare or distraction.
Make-up: natural and consistent with your everyday appearance. The photo must match your actual appearance when you pick up your card in person.

sections.title: Check Your University's Requirements Before Taking a Student ID Photo
items: Before taking or uploading any photo, go directly to your institution's card office website. Search for: [Your School Name] student ID photo requirements or [Your School Name] campus card photo upload.
Record these four things from your school's page before you take the photo:
Accepted file format (JPEG only, or JPEG and PNG, or JPEG and HEIC)
Maximum file size (this varies enormously — from 50 KB at Harvard to 2 MB at NC State)
Required or minimum image dimensions in pixels (if specified)
Background color requirement (white only, or white/light neutral, or any light solid color)

File size limits are the most commonly missed requirement. Harvard's limit of 50 KB is unusually strict — a standard phone photo taken at full resolution is typically 3–8 MB and must be compressed substantially. A photo that looks fine on your screen will be rejected by an upload portal that enforces a hard file size limit.

sections.title: Common US University Student ID Photo Requirements
items: The following specifications appear consistently across US institutions. They represent safe defaults when your school has not fully specified a particular parameter.
Specification
Standard US University Requirement
File format
JPEG (.jpg) — universally accepted. Some schools also accept PNG or HEIC. Always confirm with your institution.
File size
Varies significantly by institution: 50 KB (Harvard) to 2 MB (NC State). If not specified: target 200–500 KB.
Image dimensions
Varies: 280×296 px (Harvard), 300×400 px minimum (U Houston), 600×600 px (Northwestern). If not specified: 800×1000 px is a safe target.
Resolution
150 DPI minimum (U Iowa). If printing is involved: 300 DPI. For digital-only upload: pixel count matters more than DPI.
Background
Solid white (Harvard, most schools). Some accept any solid light/neutral color. Never patterned, never outdoors, never a room scene.
Framing / crop
Passport-style: head and shoulders. From just above the crown of your head to your collarbone. Face centered.
Head position
Directly facing the camera, head upright, not tilted or turned. Both ears at the same height.
Expression
Natural facial expression, both eyes open. Smiling is permitted at most US institutions. Extreme expressions not accepted.
Eyes
Fully open and clearly visible. Not covered by hair. If wearing glasses: no glare.
Glasses
Permitted at most institutions if eyes are clearly visible and there is no lens glare or reflection.
Head coverings
Not permitted. Exception: head coverings worn as part of daily religious or medical practice are accepted.
Attire
Neat and appropriate. Avoid white clothing (blends with white background). Avoid tube tops and spaghetti strap tops.
Digital alteration
Not permitted. No filters, AI enhancement, beauty modes, skin smoothing, or retouching of any kind.
Photo source
Must be an original digital photograph. Not a photo of a printed photo or screenshot.
Recency
The photo must represent your current appearance. Most schools review for consistency with your physical appearance when you pick up your card.

sections.title: 12 Most Common Reasons US Student ID Photos Are Rejected
items: 1. Shadow on the background. The applicant stood too close to the wall, causing their body to cast a visible shadow. Fix: stand at least 3 feet from the background.
2. Shadow on the face. A single light source from one side creates a shadow across the opposite side of the face. Fix: use two light sources or a large window facing you.
3. Head tilted. Even a slight tilt makes the photo look informal and may fail automated review. Fix: check a mirror before shooting — both ears should be at the same height.
4. Angled or profile pose. The face must face the camera directly. Any rotation is grounds for rejection.
5. Framed too tightly. Only the face is visible, no shoulders. The crop must show your head and the upper part of your shoulders — from the crown to the collarbone.
6. Colored or patterned background. Only a plain, solid white or light neutral background is accepted. Bedrooms, kitchens, outdoor settings, and patterned walls all fail.
7. Filters or digital alteration. Any filter, AI enhancement, beauty mode, or skin-smoothing is detectable and explicitly prohibited. Shoot with all enhancements turned off.
8. White shirt against white background. The clothing disappears into the background. Wear a color that contrasts with your background.
9. Hair covering the eyes. Both eyes must be fully visible. Tie back, pin, or push back any hair that falls across the eyes before shooting.
10. File too large. Especially critical at institutions with strict size limits (Harvard: 50 KB). Export at reduced JPEG quality (75–80) rather than uploading a full-resolution camera file.
11. Wrong file format. PNG submitted to a JPEG-only portal, or HEIC submitted to a portal that does not accept Apple's native format. Convert to JPEG before uploading.
12. Photo of a photo. Photographing a printed photo, screenshot, or displaying a photo on a screen and photographing that screen. All institutions require an original digital photograph.

sections.title: Making it Right: Final Thoughts on Your Student ID Photo
items: Your student ID photo is a small task, but it is one worth doing carefully. It takes less than 15 minutes to set up correctly, and getting it right the first time means your campus card is ready before you arrive — so your first day is about orientation, not waiting in a card office line.

White background, rear camera, natural light, no filters, both eyes open, and a file size that fits within your school's upload limit. That is genuinely all it takes. Check your institution's card office page for the exact specs, follow the steps in this guide, and your photo will clear review on the first submission.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
Can I Take My Student ID Photo With My Phone?
items: Yes — a smartphone is the right tool for most students. Use the rear camera (not the front-facing camera), turn off all portrait modes and beauty features, and set a self-timer so you are not holding the phone while shooting. The rear camera on a modern smartphone produces more than enough resolution and color accuracy for a campus ID photo.

sections.title: What Background do I Need for My Student ID Photo?
items: White is the safest choice for all US institutions. Most universities require white or specify a solid light/neutral color. Light gray is accepted by some schools, but not all. Blue, beige, or any non-neutral color is typically rejected. When in doubt, use white. A sheet of white poster board taped flat against a wall provides a smooth, consistent white background without needing to find a suitable wall.

sections.title: Can I Smile in My Student ID Photo?
items: Yes, at most US universities. Unlike biometric passport photos (which require a neutral expression), campus ID photos at the majority of US institutions permit a natural smile with eyes open. Check your specific school's requirements — a small number of institutions prefer a neutral expression. The most important requirement is that both eyes are fully open and clearly visible, regardless of expression.

sections.title: Can I Wear Glasses in My Student ID Photo?
items: Yes, at most US institutions. There is no general prohibition on glasses in student ID photos. The requirement is that your eyes must be clearly visible — which means no glare or reflection on the lenses, no tinted lenses or sunglasses, and no frames that cover the eyes. Anti-reflective coated lenses are much easier to photograph without glare. If you cannot eliminate lens glare in your setup, removing glasses for the photo is the simplest solution.

sections.title: What Happens if My Student Photo is Rejected?
items: Your institution's card office will notify you by email (usually to your official university email address) and ask you to submit a new photo. Your card will not be printed until a compliant photo is approved. If you are an incoming student, a rejection before arrival may mean your card is not ready for pickup on your first day of campus — which can delay access to buildings, dining, and transit services. Submit your photo early enough to allow time for a resubmission if needed.

sections.title: Can I Use an AI-Generated Photo for My Student ID?
items: No. Every US university card office that has addressed this explicitly prohibits digitally altered, AI-generated, or AI-enhanced photos. For example, the University of Iowa's guidelines specifically list photos altered by photo-editing software, apps, filters, or AI as grounds for automatic rejection. A campus ID card is an official identification document; the photo must be an authentic, unretouched representation of your current appearance.

sections.title: How is a Student ID Photo Different From a Passport Photo?
items: A passport photo is governed by strict government biometric standards with fixed dimensions, specific face-coverage percentages, and precise background color requirements. A student ID photo is governed by your institution's card office — specifications vary by school, smiling is generally permitted, file format and size limits differ significantly, and there is no standardized pixel requirement across institutions. The framing (head and shoulders, facing forward) is similar to a passport photo, but the regulatory framework is entirely different.

sections.title: Do I Need to Update My Student ID Photo?
items: Usually not. Most universities print your photo on your physical card when it is first issued. If your appearance changes significantly — a very different hairstyle, new or removed facial hair, glasses, or any change that would make you difficult to recognize from the photo — you can typically request a replacement card with a new photo from your institution's card office. Some schools charge a replacement fee; others do not. Check your institution's card replacement policy.

guides/how-to-take-passport-photo-with-i.h1: How to Take a Passport Photo With an iPhone at Home: 2026 Guide

sections.title: How to Take a Passport Photo With an iPhone at Home: 2026 Guide
items: T oday, you don't need a professional camera or a commercial studio to get an acceptable passport photo. It can be easily captured with your iPhone at home, and adapted to official passport or visa requirements with a reliable passport photo maker like PhotoGov. The digital passport photo size page shows the pixel dimensions and file limits that apply to each portal.

The key is to start with a technically solid shot: a simple home setup and a few basics are enough to capture a good original image. After that, you can turn it into a compliant ID photo in under 30 seconds with an online tool. Let's see how to do it from the comfort of your home or office (and no, you don't need the latest iPhone model).

sections.title: What iPhone Model is the Best for Taking Passport-Size Photos?
items: When it comes to passport‑size photos, you don’t actually need the newest or most expensive iPhone model to get an image that passes strict biometric checks. I use my iPhone 13 Pro to take all my visa and ID pictures, and it works just fine. However, traveling frequently and applying for different visas, I've learned that a lot depends on the quality of the original image, not the model itself. We will discuss it in detail in this post.

Pretty much all devices from the iPhone 11 and later offer fast, accurate autofocus, good performance in indoor lighting, and enough detail and sharpness to capture a clear picture without visible noise or pixelation. So don't worry if you don't have the most recent model!

Higher‑end models like the iPhone 15 or 16 series do provide a little extra dynamic range and detail. But for a small printed or digital passport photo, it's insignificant. Once the photograph has been converted to a passport-size picture with an online passport photo maker, it is virtually indistinguishable from a studio shot.
Saying that, the iPhone 17 may be a good pick if you prefer using the front camera, as many users and reviewers report noticeably sharper and cleaner selfies compared to older models.

sections.title: Front or Back Camera?
items: You can absolutely take a compliant passport photo with the front camera on an iPhone, as long as you treat the whole process like a mini-photoshoot, not as snapping a casual selfie.

The rear camera still wins for absolute sharpness and natural facial proportions , which are essential for biometric identification. The best way to capture an image with the back camera is to place the iPhone on a tripod or ask someone to take a picture of you. Maintaining a proper distance from the camera lens helps avoid typical close‑up selfie distortion that can ruin the shot by altering your face's proportions.

sections.title: Passport Photo Requirements To Follow at Home
items: The official ID photo requirements are similar worldwide. They are determined by local authorities, such as the US Department of State , or His Majesty's Passport Office in the UK. The authority behind the biometric standards that countries base their guidelines on is the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). It lists all the official requirements in Document 9303.
All passport photographs must adhere to these government standards. Below is a list of key international requirements:
A photo must be sharp and in color
A background must be plain, light, and uniform (usually white or off‑white)
An applicant's face must be presented in full, front view, looking straight at the camera
An applicant must maintain neutral expression: mouth closed, eyes open, no exaggerated expressions (smiling, frowning)
A picture must be evenly lit, with no harsh shadows or bright reflections
A photograph must be recent, typically taken within the last 6 months
Facial features, or colors, can't be digitally altered and must be presented naturally

Passport photography sizes and proportions are different for different types of documents — and there is usually an "inside" country standard for ID photos. For example, in the US, a 2 x 2-inch format is frequently used for official pictures. A UK passport photo and Schengen visa photo size is 35 x 45 mm. But you need a 43×55 mm photo for a Dubai visa. The difference in sizes, framing, and head proportion requirements can be very confusing: always double-check with the official resources or on our website before submitting your documents.

sections.title: Taking Your Own Passport Photo With an iPhone: a Step-by-Step Guide
items: Now that we've learned the basics, let’s begin the photo-making process. All you need is your iPhone and a simple setup.

sections.title: Step 1: Set up Your iPhone
items: Use the rear camera .It offers higher resolution and has better optics than the front (selfie) camera, resulting in sharper, more detailed images.

Turn off flash, filters, and portrait mode .Flash can cast shadows or create strong glare on your face — a frequent reason for ID photo rejection. Portrait mode blurs the background, and filters may alter your facial features and the colors, which are not allowed in passport photos.
Enable the grid in Camera settings . The grid will help you keep your head centered and the shot straight: a correctly proportioned image is essential for biometric identification.
Use default photo mode . Avoid Live Photos or video modes. A standard still photo at full resolution is best.

sections.title: Step 2: Create a Proper Background and Lighting Setup
items: Most passport photos get rejected because of a bad background or lighting — not because they were taken with an iPhone. Here are a few tips to create a simple home setup.
Backgroud
Choose a plain, light‑colored wall .White or very light gray works best. Avoid patterned walls, tiles, curtains, or any objects behind you.
Remove visual distractions . No frames, light switches, shelves, plants, or text in the background. For a better result, the backdrop must be clean and plain.
Lighting

Use soft, natural light .Natural daylight from a window in front of you or slightly to the side is ideal. Avoid having a bright window behind you, as it will result in an overexposed image. Similarly, don't position yourself in a dark area, as it may result in an underexposed image.
Avoid shadows and harsh light . Strong ceiling lamps or a single bright light on one side can create deep shadows on the face and background, which are not allowed on official ID photos.
Soften the light if needed . If the light is too strong, diffuse it with a sheer curtain or white fabric, so shadows under your nose and chin become softer.
A rule of thumb: if you can see clear, dark shadows around your nose, eye sockets, or behind your head, the light setup needs adjustment before you take the photo.

sections.title: Step 3: Position Yourself Correctly in the Frame
items: Biometric systems will correctly identify your face if it is centered in the frame, square to it, and within a specific size range.
Camera and Distance
Place the iPhone on a tripod or stable surface at eye level . Avoid holding the phone at arm’s length — this can result in unintentional tilt, distorted proportions, or blur.
Stand about 4–5 feet (1.2–1.5 meters) from the camera. This distance helps avoid distortion and gives enough room for the upper shoulders and head in the frame.
Use the rear camera and, if possible, ask your family member or friend to take the photo for you . If you are alone, use the timer, setting it for 3 or 10 seconds.
Your Position
Stand upright, with shoulders relaxed, facing the camera.
Keep your head straight : no tilt to the left or right, no raised or lowered chin.
Look directly into the camera lens , not at your reflection on the screen.
In the preview, your head and upper shoulders should be visible, with some space above your head and on each side. You will adjust the exact crop later.

sections.title: Step 4: Prepare Your Looks
items: Wear simple, everyday clothes in solid, darker colors that contrast with the light background. Avoid pure white tops, bold logos, busy patterns, or off‑shoulder styles that can blend into the background or look informal.

Do not wear uniforms or camouflage , and skip anything that looks like official attire. Head coverings are only allowed for religious or medical reasons if they are worn regularly and do not obscure your face.
Face and Expression
Keep a neutral facial expression .Mouth closed, eyes fully open. A subtle, natural smile (what they call "a Mona Lisa" smile) is often acceptable, but avoid any exaggerated expressions.
Don't smile, frown, or laugh . Exaggerated expressions aren't permitted in passport, visa, and ID photos.
Ensure your face is fully visible . No hair covering your eyes, eyebrows, or parts of your cheeks.
Avoid any retouching . Beauty filters and smoothing effects alter your features and will most likely cause automatic systems to flag your photo as digitally enhanced, which isn't allowed.

Remove glasses . Many authorities either require or strongly prefer photos without glasses to avoid glare and reflections. Sunglasses or any tinted lenses are not permitted in passport photos. If you must wear glasses. Only prescription glasses are allowed, and they must not have tinted lenses or thick frames that obscure your eyes. Use frames without thick rims, make sure lenses are clear and free from reflections, and keep eyes fully visible. If you need to wear glasses for medical reasons, you will need to provide a signed doctor's statement.
You may only wear head coverings if they are required for religious purposes or medical reasons and allowed by your country’s rules. Your full face must still be visible.
Aim for a polished but realistic look that matches how you normally appear during identity checks or border control.

sections.title: Step 5: Capture the Photo With iPhone
items: Activate the timer (3–10 seconds) . This eliminates camera shake and gives you time to take a suitable pose.
Tap on your face on the screen .This sets the focus and exposure correctly, making your features sharp and properly lit.
Keep still and look into the lens . Avoid blinking during the countdown. If you blink, simply repeat the shot.
Take a series of photos . Capture at least 5–10 images with the same neutral expression. This gives you options to choose the best one later.
Do not use digital zoom. If your head looks too small, move the phone slightly closer rather than zooming in, which can reduce quality.

sections.title: Step 6: Use a Passport Photo Maker to Apply Official Requirements
items: A raw iPhone photo is only the starting point for making an official ID photograph. A good passport photo maker will:
Automatically crop the photo to the correct dimensions for your chosen country and document type
Position your head and eyes within the required measurement range
Help ensure the background and margins around your face match official guidelines
Export the image in the correct resolution and file format for printing or a digital copy for online submission
This reduces the risk of small technical mistakes that lead to rejections. When an upload fails, our checklist for a rejected photo names the likely cause and the fix.

sections.title: How the Passport Photo App Fits Into the Process
items: PhotoGov is designed to create official photos that meet international ID regulations. The system uses built-in templates for 900 ID photos in over 150 countries. Just follow the steps below to convert your iPhone selfie into an application-ready photograph.
Take a series of photos on your iPhone following the guidelines above.

I f your application is of high priority , select Human Verification for an additional, manual photo check by the PhotoGov's senior compliance specialist.
Download an application-ready picture in a printable PDF format, or a digital copy for online submissions.
Instead of manually checking proportions, focus on getting a clean shot, while the passport photo maker handles the technical standards.

sections.title: Step 7: Print Your iPhone Passport Photo
items: If your passport application requires a printed high-resolution photo, the print quality must also meet specific standards. You can print the image at home — but only if you own a professional photo printer and have photographic paper of the required quality, or visit a print shop or order prints online.
Printing Options

Home printer . If you own a professional photo printer, use high‑quality photo paper (matte or glossy, depending on the requirements). Make sure printing is set to actual size (100% scale), not “fit to page”.
Local photo lab or pharmacy . Transfer the file to a USB drive or send it from your iPhone, and ask the shop to print it at the exact passport size defined by the issuing authority.
Online printing services . Check the nearest services where you can order prints, which will later be shipped to your home or office.
Do not cut into your face when trimming the photo
Keep the prints clean and flat, avoiding bends, scratches, or fingerprints
Do not laminate or alter the physical photo in any way
Well‑prepared digital files from your iPhone, combined with correct printing, usually look indistinguishable from studio‑made passport photos.

sections.title: What is the Difference Between a Digital Passport Photo and a Printable One?
items: A digital passport photo is an image file that is required for online applications. Authorities publish exact specs for pixel dimensions, aspect ratio, and maximum file size (for example, a 600×600 px JPEG under 240 kB for a U.S. online passport, or a 900×1200 px JPEG for a UK digital passport photo. You must upload the digital photo directly to an online form. The PhotoGov upload guide walks through the four US scenarios, from online renewal to a DV Lottery entry.

A printable passport photo is a physical photo printed on high-quality photo paper at a specific size (for example, 2×2 inches for U.S. passports or 50×70 mm for Canadian passports ). The printout is attached to a paper application or handed in at an embassy, consulate, or tourism agency office.

Both a digital and a printed photo must strictly adhere to international biometric standards: a plain light background, even lighting, neutral facial expression, head and shoulders centered within the shot, the head taking up about 50–80% of the image (depending on the document type).

sections.title: How to Take a Child’s Passport Photo With an iPhone
items: Child passport photos follow the same biometric rules as adults: clear, front-facing image, plain white background, even lighting without shadows. The only leniency is for newborns—some countries accept partially closed eyes if facial features are fully visible.

sections.title: Babies Who Cannot Sit Yet
items: Lay the baby on a white sheet over a firm surface. Hold the iPhone directly above, rear camera pointing straight down. Use soft window light; enable the 3–10 second timer so both hands steady the phone. Remove hats and headbands.

sections.title: Sitting Babies and Toddlers
items: Position the iPhone at eye level on a tripod, 1–1.5 meters away. Use the rear camera only. For support, use a car seat lined with white cloth (babies) or a chair against a white wall (toddlers). A helper stands behind the phone, attracting attention with a toy held near—but outside—the frame.

sections.title: iPhone Settings When Taking Passport Photos of Children
items: Tap the child's face on screen to lock focus before each shot. Avoid Portrait mode, filters, Live Photos, and flash. Keep sessions short; shoot when the child is rested.

sections.title: Processing
items: Upload to PhotoGov for automatic cropping and compliance verification.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid With iPhone Passport Photos
items: To finish, here are frequent pitfalls that cause home‑made passport photos to be rejected:
Patterned, dark, or colored background instead of plain light
Strong shadows on the face or behind the head
Use of filters, portrait mode, or heavy skin smoothing
Wrong head proportions in the final crop
Tilted head or face turned away from the camera
Glasses with reflections, tinted lenses, or frames covering the eyes
Non-religious or non-medical headwear
Wrong file size, low resolution, or incorrect print dimensions
Our examples of digital passport photos show compliant frames alongside the most common mistakes.
If you avoid these issues, your iPhone‑based passport photo stands an excellent chance of being accepted on the first try.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
Can I Really Use an iPhone Photo for a Passport?
items: Yes. Modern iPhones produce more than enough quality for passport photos as long as you follow official rules on background, lighting, composition, and sizing. In most cases, authorities care about biometric compliance, not the specific camera you use.

However, some countries still require professionally made photographs for certain documents — for example, if you're applying for a Canadian passport or citizenship, you can only provide professionally shot images, signed by a photographer or a studio.

sections.title: Do I Need a Special App to Take a Passport Photo With My iPhone?
items: You can capture the image with the built‑in Camera app, but using a dedicated passport photo maker or a passport photo app like PhotoGov simplifies cropping, sizing, and biometric checks. This reduces the risk of technical rejection even when the original shot is good (but improperly sized). The practical questions readers ask about online submissions are answered in the PhotoGov digital passport photo FAQ.

sections.title: Are Selfies Acceptable for Passport Photos?
items: Selfie‑style photos are usually not recommended because arm’s‑length shots often introduce distortion, tilt, and uneven framing. It is better to use the rear camera with a tripod, stand, or helper so the lens is at eye level and the image is straight.

sections.title: Can I Use Portrait Mode or Filters on My iPhone?
items: No. Portrait mode adds background blur, and filters or beauty effects alter the way your face looks. Passport photos must show a natural, unmodified appearance with a sharp, non‑blurred background.

sections.title: How Close Should I Stand to the iPhone?
items: A distance of about 4–5 feet (1.2–1.5 meters) works well for most iPhones. This keeps facial proportions natural and leaves enough room in the frame for correct cropping around your head and shoulders.

sections.title: How Do I Make Sure the Photo Meets U.S. Size Requirements?
items: The U.S. standard is a 2 x 2 inch photo with the head height and eye line within specific millimeter ranges. You can either set this up manually in an editor or let a passport photo maker, such as PhotoGov, automatically crop and scale the image to U.S. specifications. Please note that our service does not digitally alter facial features; it only crops and resizes images for US ID photos.

sections.title: Can I Reuse an Older iPhone Photo From My Gallery?
items: Only if it was taken within the allowed time frame (typically the last 6 months), reflects your current appearance, including hairstyle, facial hair, and is shot according to the rules listed on this page. If in doubt, take a fresh photo instead of reusing an older one.

sections.title: Do I Still Need to Go to a Photo Booth or Pharmacy if I Use PhotoGov?
items: Not necessarily. If your authority accepts digital uploads, you can submit the processed file directly. If printed photos are required, you can print the PhotoGov output at home on photo paper or send it to a local lab or pharmacy for professional printing.

sections.title: What if My iPhone Passport Photo Gets Rejected?
items: If your photo is rejected, check the reason given: common issues include background, shadows, or incorrect size. You can reshoot with adjusted lighting and positioning, then process the new image again through a passport photo maker to confirm that it meets the specified standards.

Photo 3 returned a technically compliant, biometrically aligned result, with a crop slightly tighter than the other services, and the color palette on the lighter side.

items: The most polished interface in the test. USPS print delivery available. sections.title: 1. Biometric and Compliance Filter
items: PhotoAiD does not apply a compliance check to input images. All three test photos were accepted and proceeded to payment. The service displayed "Your Photo Looks Perfect!" before checkout, though the inputs didn’t meet the biometric and the US Department of State requirements. PhotoAiD runs on the same platform as Passport Photo Online and ePassportPhoto. All three apply the same compliance behavior, interface structure, and output limitations.

sections.title: 2. Output Quality
items: Photo 1 was accepted without a compliance check and processed. PhotoAiD centred the subject within the frame but did not straighten the shoulders or head. The output returned a black border artefact. The resulting image is non-compliant with the US Department of State requirements and cannot be submitted as a passport photo.

Photo 2 produced an acceptable, sharp result with a clean background removal. The head is properly centered. The crop leaves slightly more room below the shoulders than a typical studio‑style passport photo, but this remains within the U.S. framing guidelines. The colors have a slight greenish cast. The subject’s navy tank top was kept, so the final photo may still be at risk of rejection for a U.S. passport submission.

Photo 3 produced a compliant output — centered, sharp, with a clean background removal. However, the colors appear slightly over‑saturated and more vivid than a neutral studio passport photo, and the price of the final image is higher than that of the alternative services.

items: Mid-range: $13.95 for a digital download. $16.95 for a digital download and 2 USPS printouts. PhotoAiD charges $4 more than ePassportPhoto ($9.95) for output generated by the same shared backend.

items: The most polished interface of all tested services. Clean layout, straightforward upload flow, clear document selection.

Verdict: Without a compliance check, output quality depends entirely on source photo framing. The best option for users who need physical prints and are supplying a clean, well-framed source photo.

items: USPS printout delivery available. The output depends on the input photo's quality: the service accepts selfies that do not comply with international biometric standards. Counter-intuitive interface: document selection requires scrolling to find.

The output retained the original head and torso tilt. The background hasn't been removed. The final photo returned a black frame artefact. Overall, the result is non-compliant with US passport requirements and unsuitable for official submission.

− No background removal

Verdict: The service may only be useful for cropping already compliant studio photos with a correct background. Otherwise, the output may return incompliant artifacts, backgrounds, and mismatched color profiles. Suitable for free cropping of professional passport photos.

sections.title: Watch Out! A Major Issue We’ve Encountered
items: All our input test photos contained deliberate flaws. Yet 6 out of 7 services in the test group accepted non‑compliant outputs that may compromise the whole application process. To guide the user to the most acceptable output, a passport photo maker has to flag the issue and offer a clear fix — or refuse to process the image at all.

Our 2026 testing results revealed a gap between reassuring messages like “Your photo looks perfect!” and borderline images actually being processed and charged for. Based on these findings, we encourage users to treat their input images seriously and refer to the official requirements before proceeding to payment. A good input starts with the shot itself: our guide covers making a passport photo on iPhone step by step .

guides/us-passport-photo-cost.h1: U.S. Passport Photo Cost 2026: the Most Affordable & Reliable Options

sections.title: U.S. Passport Photo Cost 2026: the Most Affordable & Reliable Options
items: Quick answer: A US passport photo costs anywhere from $0 to $17.99 depending on where you obtain it. September 2026 prices are: $7.64 for two prints at Walmart Photo; $15 at passport-photo appointments at USPS; $15.95 at FedEx Offices; $16.99 at Walgreens; and $17.99 at CVS. Taking the photo yourself and using a reliable passport photo maker is the most affordable option — for example, prices for a digital passport photo at PhotoGov start at $5.90. These prices don’t include the $130 to $195 government application fee the U.S. Department of State charges to issue the passport itself. This guide breaks down all major providers’ US passport photo costs in 2026. Our experts break down the most reliable options so you can make an informed decision and avoid a rejection.
US Passport Photo Prices in 2026: a Detailed Comparison Table

The table below lists the current price for a standard 2 x 2 inch US passport photo at every major provider, sourced directly from their official pricing pages. All prices below are current for September 2026.

sections.title: Passport Photo Prices at CVS, Walgreens, and Walmart
items: Pharmacies and big-box retailers are the most common stop for a U.S. passport photo, mainly because of their convenient locations and easy walk-ins. Prices vary by over $10 for two prints.

sections.title: CVS Passport Photo Price
items: CVS charges $17.99 for two 2 x 2 inch prints, taken and printed in-store with no appointment. A digital copy sent by email costs an additional $3.99, and a copy saved to a Kodak Moments USB drive costs $10.99. CVS includes a verification certificate confirming the photo meets government size and background standards, and the store will retake a rejected photo free of charge if you bring back your receipt.

sections.title: Walgreens Passport Photo Price
items: Walgreens charges $16.99 for the full passport photo service, which includes two prints and a free digital copy delivered by email. Photos are ready within a few minutes, with the full visit usually taking an hour or less. A USB copy is available for an added fee on top of the base price.

sections.title: Walmart Passport Photo Price
items: Walmart Photo is $7.64 for two 2 x 2 inch prints — the lowest price among major in-store retailers. You can upload your photo online for same-day pickup in about an hour, or have it taken in-store. Walmart does not list a bundled digital-copy fee on the same page; the $7.64 covers the printed photos.

sections.title: Passport Photo Prices at USPS, The UPS Store, and FedEx Office
items: Shipping and postal counters offer passport photos as a side service alongside their passport application help, and pricing is less standardized than at pharmacies.

sections.title: USPS Passport Photo Price
items: U.S. passport photo at USPS costs $15 for two prints at its in-person and appointment-based services. Keep in mind that not every post office offers photo service, and locations that do typically require an appointment; use the USPS location finder to confirm a nearby office offers it before you go. The $15 fee is entirely separate from the $35 execution fee USPS charges to process your passport application in person.

sections.title: The UPS Store Passport Photo Price
items: The UPS Store does not have a single national price for passport photo production. Individual store listings show a range: one Charlotte, North Carolina location lists $19.99 for two prints and $34.99 for prints plus a digital copy, while other stores list prices closer to $12 to $14. Call ahead or check your specific store's page, since the cost at one UPS Store can run nearly three times the price at another.

sections.title: FedEx Office Passport Photo Price
items: FedEx Office charges $15.95 for a passport photo, available as a print, a digital file, or both (per office.fedex.com , checked August 2026). No appointment is required at a staffed location. FedEx Office also sells separate passport-application expediting packages starting at $119 plus government fees, which is a different service from the photo itself and is easy to confuse with it while booking.

sections.title: Does Costco Still Take Passport Photos?
items: Costco's Photo Center does not currently provide a standalone in-store passport service. We recommend using other shops or designated photo studios in your area. If you want to save time on a studio visit, you can always make a passport photo from the comfort of your home by using an online passport photo tool.

sections.title: Passport Photo Prices at a Photo Studio
items: Passport photo prices at a professional (commercial) photo studio vary depending on many factors — from location to reputation, from the service range to the photographer’s experience. Expect to pay as low as $20 and as high as $100 for a professional photoshoot. Always inquire about the final price before booking your appointment.

sections.title: Why Passport Photos Cost More at a Counter Than at Home
items: A standard 4 x 6 inch glossy print costs $0.42 at CVS, and similar per-print pricing applies at other pharmacy photo counters. The $15 to $18 most retailers charge for a passport photo mostly pays for a staff member's time. That covers positioning you against the background, taking the shot, running it through compliance-checking software like the system CVS describes on its passport photo page, and reprinting it if the first attempt fails.

That gap is also why bringing your own already-cropped, compliant file and printing it as a standard photo, rather than paying for the staffed "passport photo" service, can cut the cost by more than 40 times. The next section walks through exactly how.

sections.title: How to Get a Passport Photo for Under $1
items: A 4 x 6 inch print holds two 2 x 2 inch images side by side with room to spare. Create a compliant passport photo yourself, arrange two copies on a 4 x 6 canvas, and order it as a standard photo print instead of the staffed passport photo service. The print itself costs $0.42 at CVS, plus a fee that a photo tool charges to generate the file.
How to take your own passport photo at home:
Take the photo against a plain white or off-white wall, in even light, with a neutral expression and both eyes open.
Crop and size the image to 2 x 2 inches at 600 x 600 pixels using a free tool or an app that checks the crop against the size and background rules automatically.
Arrange two copies of the cropped image on a single 4 x 6 inch canvas using any basic photo-editing or collage tool.
Upload the 4 x 6 file as a standard PDF file, and print it at a local print shop or photo lab.
After printing, cut the two photos apart with scissors or a paper cutter along a straight edge.

Making a photo by yourself is the easiest and time-saving way, but it leaves the compliance check entirely up to you. If you’re only printing the file at a shop, the staff at the print counter won’t verify the size, background, or expression. Therefore, it is recommended to run the file through a checker before you print it.

items: The price you pay for a passport photo has nothing to do with the U.S. Department of State passport issuing fee. Below are the current issuing fees for different types of U.S. passports.

sections.title: Passport Photo Costs for Babies and Children
items: A passport photo for a baby or child costs the same base price as an adult photo at nearly every retailer and online tool listed above. The cost difference may come from the number of attempts while taking an actual photo. See US baby and child passport photo rules for the specific requirements that make a child's photo harder to get right on the first try, including the neutral-expression rule and the restriction on anyone else appearing in the frame. Use our convenient Baby passport photo tool to escape a visit to the photo shop.

sections.title: Who Doesn't Need to Pay for a New Passport Photo
items: If you have a fully compliant passport-size photo that has been taken within the past six months, you may not need to capture a new one. If it matches all current US Passport Photo Requirements , you can submit it digitally or print it out on photo-quality paper for in-person submission.

sections.title: Avoiding a Second Passport Photo Charge
items: A rejected passport photo does not just cost time. If you paid $15 to $18 at a counter for a photo that gets flagged during application review, and mailed a paper application, you will need to pay for a second photo and wait for a new one to arrive before your application can move forward. That delay stacks on top of standard passport processing time.

Checking a photo against the official size, background, and expression rules before you submit it removes that risk. A tool like PhotoGov checks a photo against the current specification before you download or print it, which catches an off-center crop, a shadowed background, or a wrong pixel count before a government reviewer does, rather than after you have already paid for a print.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
What Is the Cheapest Way to Get a Passport Photo?
items: Taking the photo yourself at home and printing it as a standard 4 x 6 photo сan cost you under $1 in print fees. But keep in mind that this option puts you at risk of non-compliance. It is safer to use a reliable passport photo checker that will compare your photo to all current requirements and adjust it, if needed. Among the “offline” providers, Walmart Photo is the least expensive at $7.64 for two prints.

sections.title: Is Getting a Passport Photo at USPS Free?
items: No. USPS charges $15 for appointment-based passport photo services. This fee is separate from the $35 processing USPS fee for in-person passport applications.

sections.title: Does CVS or Walgreens Charge More for a Passport Photo?
items: It depends on what you compare it with. Prices at CVS and Walgreens are higher than most online photo-making tools, and more than double what Walmart Photo charges. At CVS, two copies cost $17.99, plus $3.99 extra for a digital file, and at Walgreens — $16.99 for two prints and a free digital copy by email.

sections.title: Can I Reuse an Old Passport Photo to Save Money?
items: Yes, but only if it was taken within the last six months and still meets the current requirements. A photo taken more than six months ago, or one that no longer looks like you, has to be retaken regardless of how well it met the rules when it was taken (per travel.state.gov , checked August 2026).

sections.title: How Much Does a Passport Photo Cost for a Baby or Child?
items: A baby or child passport photo costs the same as an adult photo: from about $5.90 with an online tool to $17.99 at CVS, depending on the provider. The only thing that can increase the price is the need for a retake — sometimes it takes more than one visit to get a sufficient photo. That’s the reason online tools make so much sense for children’s passport photos.

sections.title: Is the Passport Photo Fee Included in the Passport Application Fee?
items: No. The $130 to $195 the U.S. Department of State charges to issue a passport does not include the price for capturing a photo at a studio or with an online tool.

sections.title: Does It Cost More to Get a Digital Passport Photo Than a Printed One?
items: Usually, yes, but not if you’re using an online passport photo maker. CVS charges $3.99 extra for a digital copy on top of its $17.99 print price, and Walgreens includes a digital copy for free. Online tools typically deliver a digital file as the base product (sometimes it’s free, sometimes at an affordable price), with printing as the optional extra step.

sections.title: Is It Cheaper to Use an Online Passport Photo Tool Than a Store?
items: In most cases, yes. A free or low-cost digital file from a tool like PhotoGov, printed as a standard photo for $0.42 to $1 at a pharmacy, costs under $10, and well under the $15 to $18 that USPS, FedEx Office, Walgreens, or CVS charge for their passport photo service.

sections.title: How Can I Get a Compliant Passport Photo Without Overpaying?
items: Take the photo at home against a plain background, run it through a compliance check with a reliable online passport photo maker, and print it on high-quality photo paper — or simply download a digital file if you’re applying online.
